a-year-of-earthquakes-played.text: got it: drop it from wave 1? it was one of the three shwarms with an author sign-off (a20). if you say yes, i'll move it out, promote a wave-2 shwarm in its place (suggest 'every freedoom map, proven beatable' or 'the bayeux tapestry in ascii'), and give the author check to another wave-1 shwarm so we still test sign-off three times. or tell me what to change instead.
it just doesnt feel like something that would require an entire shwarm. other ideas?

agreed, one person could do that in a weekend. bigger ideas that genuinely need a crowd, same earthquake spirit: (1) recommended, 'a seismograph in 100 homes': an open design for a home seismometer under $100 (a geophone or accelerometer plus a raspberry pi), built by people in their own houses in at least 10 countries, all streaming to one open map. done when: at least 100 home-built stations in 10+ countries stream to a public server, and the network detects at least 20 magnitude 4+ earthquakes that usgs also logs, each within 60 seconds of usgs's origin time, from the open data alone. it can still play the quakes as sound on the live map. that's hardware, software, and people everywhere: a real shwarm. (2) 'the dawn chorus of the world': people in 50 countries record the same 10 minutes of sunrise birdsong on the same day, and an open model names every species in every recording, checked against birdnet and human birders. (3) 'earthquake early warning for one city': phones and home sensors in one quake-prone city (e.g. lima or kathmandu) give a 5-second warning before shaking arrives, shown in a replay of a real quake. pick one (or none) and i'll write the full card. it keeps the author sign-off either way.

1 a shwarm shouldnt end in a homebrew pi kit. any piece fo hardware designed for distribution to as many people as possible must include research, design and distribution of a completely finished and cost optimized product. please update any other shwarms like this. otherwise, yes i approve.

2 no. but im still on board with training a geolocation model based on birdsong

3 yeah i guess, it could build on #1. but it should be to distribute to as many cities as possible. honestly, this should BUILD ON the device shwarm.

approving #1 with your rule: a finished, cost-optimized home seismometer (research, design, distribution), not a pi kit. i'll write it as a new card, then sweep the list for other hardware shwarms that end in a kit and fix them the same way. #3 (early warning in as many cities as possible) goes on the ideas list to build on the device shwarm once it passes. birdsong geolocation: i'll check it's on the ideas list.

printer-motor-orchestra.text: actually no. make multiple 3d printers TALK using TTS. like that piano that they programmed to talk

yes, much better. that's the peter ablinger move (his 'speaking piano' splits a voice into frequencies and has a robot hand play them). printers can do it the same way: break a recorded voice into its loudest frequencies every few milliseconds, give each stepper motor one of them, and the room says the words. proposed rewrite. title: 'printers that talk'. what: 'a stepper motor hums whatever pitch you spin it at, and every 3d printer has four. split a spoken sentence into its strongest frequencies, many times a second, hand one to each motor, and a room of printers can say words out loud. ablinger did it with a piano and a robot hand; nobody has done it with printers.' done when: 'an unedited single-take video shows at least 4 3d printers, making sound only with their own stepper motors, saying a public-domain sentence of at least 12 words, and the open whisper model (large-v3) transcribes the audio with a word error rate under 40%.' checked by: 1 run (whisper wer script on the recording) + 1 human who listens without the script first and writes down what they hear. tweaks welcome: the word count, the error rate, or a fixed sentence (e.g. 'daisy, daisy, give me your answer do', the first song a computer sang). say yes and i'll rewrite the card and its sources.
correction: i wrote 'nobody has done it with printers' without checking. i'll search for prior talking-printer or stepper-motor speech projects before i write the final card, and say what i find.
again though, it doesnt seem like something that goes beyond what someone would be able to do with their max plan...thoughts?

you're right: one person with a few printers and a max plan could do the talking version alone. what makes it a shwarm is printers nobody owns alone. 'the printer choir': like eric whitacre's virtual choir, but with 3d printers in people's homes. each owner gets one voice part (a few frequencies of the same sentence or song), records their printer playing it to a shared click track, and the parts are lined up into one recording that speaks or sings. done when: at least 50 printers in at least 10 countries, each filmed unedited in its owner's home playing its own part, add up to one recording of a public-domain song (e.g. 'daisy bell', the first song a computer sang) that the open whisper model transcribes with under 30% word error, every part's video and g-code linked. that needs dozens of strangers with printers, which no single plan can buy. if that's still not it, drop it and i'll replace it. also: i'll re-read all 100 with your bar ('could one person with a max plan just do this?') and flag the ones that fail, so you don't have to catch them one by one.
you know what would be wild, shwarming the largest 3d printed object? maybe guinness world record for largest benchy printed in one week? something like that
but no, anything that can be hacked into a print farm, still just a basement project

got it, no benchy: anything a print farm could do alone is a basement project. should i drop this card, or bring back one idea where the crowd is people in many places (not more printers)? i'll hold it until you say.

mosquito-hearing-chip.text: why do we want to do this? are there species more dangerous than others? can you detect if they have malaria by how they sound?

good questions. why: malaria kills about 600,000 people a year, mostly young children in africa (who's yearly report), and dengue infects millions more. health teams fight it by knowing which mosquitoes are where and when, so they know where to spray and hand out nets. today that means trapping them and having an expert identify them under a microscope, which is slow and scarce. a $5 sensor that hears them could map that automatically, day and night. that's the point of the humbug project this builds on. which species: yes, hugely. of about 3,500 mosquito species, only some anopheles species carry malaria (and only the females bite). aedes aegypti carries dengue, zika and yellow fever; culex carries west nile. most species are harmless nuisances. can you hear malaria: not as far as i know. no reliable sound signature for infection has been shown; what sound can do is tell the species apart, and the species tells you the risk. so a sharper version of this shwarm: 'tell malaria-carrying anopheles apart from every other mosquito, on a $5 chip'. humbugdb has species labels for that. want me to rewrite it that way? i'd check the latest numbers and papers before writing the final card.
hold on you know what would be pretty cool? a model trained to geolocate you based on the bird sounds it can hear. theres already models for identifying birds, we just gotta train the geolocation

that's a great one: geoguessr by ear. and it's crowd-sized for a real reason: the test needs fresh recordings from all over the world that nobody trained on. sketch. title: 'where am i? ask the birds.' what: 'bird models can already name the species singing outside your window. the mix of species, and even their regional accents, says a lot about where on earth you are. train an open model that hears one minute of outdoor sound and guesses where it was recorded.' done when: 'an open model, trained only on openly licensed recordings, places at least 200 new one-minute outdoor recordings, made after the shwarm opens by at least 50 people in at least 20 countries and hidden from the model, with a median error under 500 km.' checks: 1 run (scores the model on the hidden set) + 1 human who records their own minute and checks the guess. two license notes: birdnet's model is non-commercial, so it can't be the base; google's perch bird model is apache-licensed and works. and xeno-canto recordings must be filtered to cc by / by-sa / cc0. one care note: it should guess a region (hundreds of km), never a street. two questions: should this replace the mosquito shwarm, or be its own new one (and which wave)?

no more lobbies, but the done criteria can be at least so many recordings and successful location by three people in different parts of the world.

non-commercial. whats wrong with that? also, thats not a criteria we have to worry about it. if its accessible media, then the shwarm can pick it. if someone wants to pay for licensing on something, that's up to the shwarm.

replace the mosquito shwarm

got it: the birdsong one replaces the mosquito card. done when: at least a set number of new recordings from around the world, and three people in different parts of the world each record their own and the model places them correctly. no license rule on the card: the shwarm picks its data and models, non-commercial ones included. i'll write it up and put it here for your approval.

trappist-1-blind-search.text: has this not been done? if so, then hell yeah

honest answer: it has been done. luger et al. found the seventh planet's 18.77-day orbit in exactly this k2 data in 2017 (that's the paper the done test checks against), though they knew the inner six from spitzer first. so this shwarm is a rediscovery, not new science: can an open crew, starting from raw pixels and not peeking, find all seven on their own? the payoff is an open, step-by-step notebook anyone can learn planet hunting from, and a test of whether a crowd plus agents can redo a nature paper from scratch. if that's enough of a hell yeah, approve it and i'll make the pitch say 'rediscover' plainly so nobody thinks it's a new find. if you'd rather have something unsolved, say so and i'll look for an open, still-unanswered search in public telescope data to put in its place.
done: title now 'rediscover all seven trappist-1 planets in raw k2 pixels', and the pitch says plainly it's a rediscovery that leaves an open notebook behind. done test unchanged.

where-the-grocery-stores-went.text: to see which towns lost their grocery store, and when. when the last supermarket in a town closes, people drive 20 miles for food or live on dollar-store shelves, and that shows up in health and in who stays. today nobody has an open, year-by-year record of it: usda's food access atlas is a snapshot, and usda has stopped updating its snap data system. this table would let a local reporter write 'our county lost 4 of its 6 grocery stores since 2010', let a city council or nonprofit back a grant to bring one back, and let researchers line it up with health or population data. if the pitch doesn't make that clear, i can rewrite 'what' to lead with it (e.g. 'when a town's last grocery store closes, nobody keeps the record. usda's retailer file does, by accident...') and add a per-county page a reporter can quote. want that, or approve as is?
lets be sure to include the why. honestly all of these are better when theres a why

done: the pitch now opens with the why (towns losing their last store, no public record, what a reporter, a town and researchers can do with it), and the done test adds a page per county a reporter can quote. and noted for all of them: every pitch should lead with its why. i'll do a why pass on the rest once you've been through wave 1, together with the crowd-sized fixes.

rust-coreutils-last-tests.text: i dont get it but im not knowledgeable. rust rewrites of linux tools? anyway, they recently converted adobe tools to rust, we should convert all of linux to rust..?

plain version: every linux computer has a set of tiny commands (ls, cp, sort, cat…) that nearly everything else runs on. they were written in c decades ago. uutils rewrote them in rust, which rules out whole classes of memory bugs, and ubuntu now ships it by default. it's almost there: it fails 51 of the original tools' 703 tests, each a small real bug. this shwarm closes most of them, so ubuntu's rust tools behave exactly like the old ones. on the adobe news: i can't confirm that one. on 'all of linux in rust': that's a great root shwarm, and a goal tree is exactly how shwarm handles something that big. the kernel already takes rust drivers, sudo has a rust rewrite (sudo-rs) and redox is a whole os written in rust. a checkable version: 'a bootable ubuntu image where coreutils, findutils, diffutils, sudo and the shell utilities are all rust, passing each original project's test suite at 99% or better.' this coreutils shwarm then becomes its first branch. want me to add that as a new shwarm with this one under it, or keep this one as is?
ok, buuut im not talkig tools. im talking the kernel, tools, whatever--i have no idea why we want to do it, i just know theres some murmur about how insane that would be.

got it: the whole thing, kernel and all. here's the why in plain words: most serious security holes in big c programs are memory mistakes (microsoft and google's chrome team each put it near 70%), and rust rules most of those out. linux is written in c, runs most of the world's servers and phones, and only lets rust in at the edges today. rewriting all of it is the 'insane' part people murmur about. a checkable version: a linux-compatible kernel written in rust (projects like asterinas have started) that boots and runs ordinary linux programs unchanged, with a rust userland on top, passing a big share of the linux test project. that needs hundreds of people on drivers, filesystems and tests, so it's truly crowd-sized. i'll research it and write the card to replace this one (the coreutils piece can be one of its branches later), then put it here for your approval.

the-hand-drawn-world.text: i dont really get it. however, you could make this a hand drawn map of the world where people can submit their own drawn maps of their neighborhood and match it up to google maps or something.

fair, the pixel-tile version is abstract. yours is warmer: people draw their own neighborhood by hand, and it gets pinned to the real map. one change: match it to openstreetmap, not google maps (google's terms don't allow copying or overlaying like this; osm is open and made for it). proposed rewrite. title: 'the hand-drawn world'. what: 'everyone carries a map of their own neighborhood in their head. draw yours by hand, on paper or screen, the way you'd sketch it for a friend. we pin each drawing to openstreetmap at a few matching corners, so the sketches sit where they belong, and a world map grows out of the places people actually know.' done when: 'a public web map shows at least 30 hand-drawn neighborhood maps by 30 different people in at least 5 countries, each warped onto openstreetmap from at least 4 matching points with an average error under 25 meters, every drawing under an open license.' checked by: 1 run (script that recomputes each drawing's error from its matching points) + 1 human who opens the map and compares 10 random drawings with the street layout. the drawings live where the crew keeps them (e.g. wikimedia commons) and are linked, since shwarm holds only text. it keeps its author sign-off. say yes or tweak the numbers.
done: rewritten as 'the hand-drawn world' (new slug the-hand-drawn-world), with the done test above, author sign-off kept, osm and qgis/gdal as sources.

done, rewritten as '100 landmark flash games, playing again'. leads with the why (a generation's games went dark in 2020), and the done test: 100 landmark games, picked by at least 20 people's nominations and votes, all play through their first level in ruffle, each confirmed by 2 players, every needed fix merged in ruffle, and each playable at a stable internet archive page. one care note added: a game goes onto the archive only if it's already there or its maker agrees. (note: waves 2 and 3 open after launch, so no rush on these; i'll recheck the ruffle numbers before it's posted.)

every-freedoom-map-beatable.text: approved. quick check: as written, or with the crowd-sized version from the crowd check (each of the 68 maps gets 3 blind first-play demos from 3 different players, and every softlock they find is fixed upstream)? i'll assume the crowd-sized one unless you say otherwise, since as written one good player could do it alone.

500-nouns-in-16-pixels.text: update all of our things with a why. cuz...why?

on it: four agents are rewriting every pitch (all 100) so it opens with its why. this card gets one too, and if the honest why is thin i'll flag it for you to drop or reshape. you'll see the new text on each card when they're done.
ok but...is this words or pictures? thats what i dont get.

pictures. one tiny picture per word: a 16×16 dot drawing of a dog for 'dog', a cup for 'cup', and so on, for the 500 most common nouns. the words only decide what gets drawn. the test is whether people can name each picture: shown one, they pick the right word out of 4 choices. (the drawings live on the shwarm's own repo and are linked; shwarm itself stores only the text.) i'll make the card's first line say that plainly: '500 tiny pictures, one for each of the 500 most common nouns.'

game-boy-cartridge.text: i honestly dont think this is something that hasnt been done? loading a rom to a cartridge isnt that hard?

you're right that flashing a rom onto a cartridge is easy, and making a game boy game has been done a thousand times. the hard part was meant to be the game, not the cartridge, but as written (a 30-minute game) one person can do it alone. the crowd check suggests: a 3-hour adventure with 20 areas, each area's art and music by a different contributor, played to the credits by 5 people on original hardware. honestly, even that is a fun-sized project more than a meaningful one. i'd drop it unless the crowd version excites you. say 'no' to drop, or 'yes' for the crowd version.

minecraft-in-doom-survival.text: approved, noted. one dependency: minecraft in doom itself is being rethought (your freedoom-episode-1-in-blocks idea, waiting on its card). once that's settled i'll rewrite this survival variant to match, so the two stay one family.

a-clock-set-by-the-stars.text: could we create a model that can identify a dark starry sky using a simple array of very sensitive pxels? a blurry array should be enough to determine the sky its looking at?

yes, and it's a better shwarm than the clock. satellites already do this with 'star trackers': a small camera finds a few bright stars and matches their pattern against a catalog to know exactly which way it's pointing. they cost thousands. a blurry, very low-res array can still work, because it only needs the brightest handful of stars and their angles, not detail; the hard parts are noise, clouds, light pollution and a tiny lens. once it knows the sky it's looking at plus the time, it knows which way is north and roughly your latitude, with no gps. sketch: 'a $20 star compass'. done when: an open design under $20 in parts, with a sensor of at most 64x64 pixels, gives heading within 2 degrees and latitude within 1 degree on clear nights, tested by at least 30 builders in at least 10 countries against their phone's gps, every result logged. the crowd is the point: skies, latitudes and light pollution nobody can test alone. want me to rewrite the card that way?

printed-pipe-organ.text: hmm, how about a 3d printed...horn or trumpet or something, that is generationally generated to be as close to matching as possible to a professional counterpart, but printed in PLA

love it. plastic trumpets already exist (you can buy them), but they don't sound like a good brass one. the open question is whether design can close the gap: let a computer evolve the inside shape of the tube and bell (what players call the bore) in an acoustics simulation until its resonances match a professional trumpet's, then print it in pla. the crowd part is real: dozens of different printers (does it still work when someone else prints it?), players to test how it plays, and blind listeners. sketch: 'a pla trumpet you can't tell from brass'. done when: an open, simulation-evolved trumpet design, printed in pla by at least 20 people on their own printers, has its first 8 resonances within 10 cents of a professional brass trumpet's on every print, and in a blind test of recordings by the same players, at least 50 listeners pick the plastic one no better than chance (under 60% right). checks: a run that measures resonances from a recording of a frequency sweep, plus a human player's verdict. want me to rewrite the card that way?

see-your-alpha-waves.text: yes! more stuff like this. research project into making gauges, meters and scopes through printing, off the shelf parts, or generation techniques.

great direction. a root shwarm for it, with branches: 'the open home lab: 20 real scientific instruments under $50 each'. done when: 20 open instrument designs (printed parts, off-the-shelf electronics, or computer-generated shapes), each built by at least 5 people in different places and each matching a professional instrument within a stated tolerance on the same samples. branch ideas, each its own done test: a spectrometer from a printed body and a diffraction grating, checked against a lab spectrometer's lines; an oscilloscope from a cheap microcontroller, checked against a bench scope; a microscope that resolves 1 micron (we already have five-strangers-one-microscope); a ph meter, a light meter calibrated against an sqm, a seismometer (the 100-homes idea), a geiger counter, a soil moisture meter (the $2 sensor shwarm), this alpha-wave eeg. a few of these are already in waves 2–3, so they'd become its first branches. want me to add the root shwarm and list the branches under it?

weigh-the-earth-on-a-table.text: approved. to make it crowd-sized i'd give it the open-home-lab shape: an open torsion balance under $50, built by at least 10 people in different places, whose measurements of g average within 5% of the accepted value. it could be a branch of the home lab root if you add that. i'll apply that version unless you say otherwise.

all-of-ubuntu-in-rust.text: nope. all of linux. and perhaps a specific distribution. arch?

yes: all of linux, kernel included, and arch is a good pick (small base, rolling, its own test-friendly packages). i'll fold this into the rust card i'm writing: arch's base system and a linux-compatible kernel, all in rust, booting and running arch's own packages unchanged.

the-dawn-chorus-of-the-world.text: i guess thats pretty cool. whats the output? a video? this seems like an art project.

honest answer: the output is a map and an open archive: thousands of same-morning recordings, each pinned to a place, with every species named by a model and checked by birders. that's a one-day snapshot of which birds sing where, which scientists can compare year to year. but you're right that the pull is mostly artistic. my suggestion: drop it as its own card and make its recordings day part of 'where am i? ask the birds': the people recording the dawn chorus are exactly the fresh test set that shwarm needs. ok?

a-seismometer-in-100-homes.text: fair push. the sensing chip itself can be that cheap: a basic accelerometer is $1–3, and a wifi chip (esp32) is about $2–3. but a finished thing you plug in also needs a board, a power supply, a case, assembly, testing and shipping, and shipping alone is often $3–8 a box. the cheapest chips are also too noisy to feel a distant magnitude 4 quake, so the shwarm would need better ones (around $5–15). my honest estimate: $20–30 each, all in, at a run of a few thousand. i'd set the done test at under $25 all in, which beats today's finished options ($585 for a raspberry shake, about $50 for openeew's kit) by a lot. ok to use $25? (the card is also moving to 1000 homes, per your note.)
